scenes.text: Quick question. An agent can now write a working piece of a billing system in an afternoon. So in a big system today, what's scarce? [pause] Code? Servers? Or knowing that what got built is right? [pause] <emphasis>Knowing it's right.</emphasis> Code got cheap. Checking it didn't. [pause] Thirty years ago, the answer was very different.

scenes.text: I've been building systems for about thirty years. Systems built around money: electronic rent payments, a card-issuing platform, an investment adviser for nonprofits. And systems that sell: retail e-commerce and E.D.I., subscription billing, and today, e-commerce again. [pause] And the way you build a big system keeps changing.

data.label: ABOUT THIRTY YEARS OF BUILDING SYSTEMS
data.caption: Payments, cards, billing, investing, commerce.

scenes.text: Here's a useful way to see why. <slow>Architecture bends around whatever is scarcest.</slow> Whatever is expensive, or slow, the design works around it. So for each of four eras, ask: what was scarce?

data.headline:
A useful lens: architecture
bends around whatever
is scarcest.

scenes.text: Thirty years ago, the commercial web was brand new. You bought servers and racked them yourself, and more capacity was weeks away. So, typically, you built one big program, on one big database, and shipped a few times a year. Companies traded orders as overnight batch files, through E.D.I., and much of that still runs. [pause] What was scarce? <emphasis>The machines.</emphasis>

scenes.text: Ten years ago. The cloud, by default, for new systems. Many small services, in containers, owned by small teams. The best teams deployed many times a day. And parts they once built themselves became a service, behind an A.P.I. [pause] What was scarce? <emphasis>Seeing the whole.</emphasis> No one person could hold it all in their head, so we built dashboards and tracing to see it.

scenes.text: Now a made-up example: a subscription-billing system, built today, the kind of platform I ran as C.T.O. at sticky dot I O. Clear modules, with boundaries an agent can work inside. One repository, where it can find anything. Tests and specs it can check itself against. And decisions written down, because the agent wasn't in the meeting. [pause] My own team keeps its code that way: one repository, with instruction files for the agents.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  A SUBSCRIPTION-BILLING SYSTEM, BUILT NOW
data.caption: Boundaries an agent can work inside. Checks it can run.

scenes.text: I'll be straight about that list. It's where the thinking is heading, not a settled answer. The evidence for it is still thin, and indirect. Every era had a confident answer, then found its costs.

data.headline:
Where the thinking is heading.
Not settled.

scenes.text: And here's what never changed, in any era. The data model outlives the code. Money has to add up. Every system depends on things you don't control: a bank, a card network, a partner's system. And somebody has to understand the layer below.

data.label: WHAT NEVER CHANGED  ·  TRUE IN ALL FOUR ERAS

items.text: The data model outlives the code
items.sub: Programs get rewritten. The data stays.
Every rent payment, card transaction, renewal

items.text: You depend on what you don’t control
items.sub: A bank, a card network, a partner’s system
When it breaks, someone has to look underneath

scenes.text: Here's the path. Today, the four eras. Then, build a whole system A.I. native, decompose it, and run agents in parallel. Then governance, quality, skills, and pipelines. [pause] And finally, agents that operate enterprise systems.

data.label: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING 201  ·  FROM LOOP TO ENTERPRISE SYSTEMS
rows: Decompose the system into a graph

scenes.text: So, to recap. Architecture bends around what's scarce. Today, that's knowing the work is right, and context. So design for checking. And the four constants still hold.

data.headline: Four eras, one lens
items: Now: knowing it’s right, and context
So design for checking: boundaries, tests

scenes.text: Which gives us rule one, for your agents. Before you design a system, write down four things. Where the boundaries are. What the data model is. What you depend on, and don't control. And how you'll know it's right. Then put it in the repository, where every agent can read it.

lines.text: Before you design a system, write down:
what you depend on and don’t control,
and how you’ll know it’s right.
Put it in the repo, where every agent can read it.

data.foot: THE FULL RULE IS ON THE LESSON PAGE

scenes.text: Now, your turn. Pick the oldest system you still depend on. When was it built, and what was scarce back then? [pause] Then ask your A.I. which era's thinking is hiding inside it.
